segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So let's make a little recap of some of the situations in which we are using the mood tense with a new verb, dejar. Dejar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Dejar means to leave, but in the sense of to leave a message rather than leave to go out like salir. Dejar.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Dejar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Dejar, good. How would you say leave me a message speaking formally? A message is un mensaje, un mensaje.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Déjeme un mensaje... mensaje.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Déjeme un mensaje. And of course, positive command, we have the me (me) after the verb. Déjeme un mensaje.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say I want you to leave me a message speaking informally? I want you to leave me a message.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero que me dejes un mensaje.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Quiero que me dejes un mensaje. In the same way, if you were to say I want to tell him to leave me a message, you won't say I want to tell him to leave me a message literally, you would say I want to tell him that he leaves me a message. What is to say or to tell?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Decir.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Decir, good. So, I want to tell him is the first bit.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero decirle...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: ...that he leaves me a message.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ...que deje, me deje un mensaje.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Quiero decirle que me deje un mensaje. So you don't want to tell him that he is leaving you a message, you want to tell him to leave you a message. So here we use the mood tense. No? If you were to say Quiero decirle que me deja un mensaje, what would be understood there without the mood tense is I want to tell him that he, she, or you formal is leaving me a message. But if you use here your mood tense, then it's understood there that sense of order and you will understand I want to tell him to leave me a message: Quiero decirle que me deje un mensaje. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: When he leaves you the message, call me. Let's speak informally. When he leaves you the message, call me.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Cuando te deje el mensaje...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Cuando te deje el mensaje, call me, informally. So it's our shortcut.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Llámame.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Cuando te deje el mensaje, or cuando él te deje el mensaje if you wanted to clarify, llámame. Good. So after cuando, when we're referring to the future, when we're referring to something that hasn't happened yet, we feel a bit superstitious about it and we want to use our mood tense: Cuando te deje el mensaje, llámame. It's essential that he sees my message. It is essential, the -tial here, what do you think might happen to it in Spanish? Like the -tion, like in tradition, becomes...

segments.speaker: Student

segments.text: So something similar might happen here.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Esencial.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Well done. Esencial. Spatial: espacial. Good. So, it's essential that he sees my message.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es esencial que...

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: He sees my message. It's based on the irregularity of veo, the I version.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Vea.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So it's essential that he or she or you formal see my message.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Es esencial que vea mi mensaje.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Es esencial que vea mi mensaje. Good. Ojalá in Spanish means something like hopefully. Ojalá.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ojalá.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You will hear it a lot, ojalá. And there's a lot of versions of the history of where it came from. What it's definitely got something to do with is Allah, the Arabic word for God, or the God, Allah. And the south of Spain was part of the Muslim world for for around eight centuries, so we have a lot of Arabic words and structures and habits in Spanish. And one of them is this popular expression ojalá. And there's a lot of versions of where it came from exactly, although my favorite is that it's a contraction of ojo Allah. Ojo means eye, and it's still used in some places like watch out, ¡ojo! ¡Ojo, eh! Careful! Watch it! Beware! So it's like ojo Allah. So you say it when you want something: ojo Allah, I want this. Ojalá. Hopefully. Although that's just one version of where ojalá came from.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So after ojalá, you can use the mood tense to say what you want to happen. So you can say, for example, hopefully she will leave a message or she leaves a message using your mood tense. Hopefully she leaves a message.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ojalá deje un mensaje.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Ojalá deje un mensaje. How would you say hopefully it will be soon? When something happens is a characteristic of it, so if we want to say hopefully it's soon, we need to use that irregular root of ser that we have in the mood tense. Do you remember how that is? And it's like the popular expression that we have in Spanish that you might hear a lot which begins o-.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: O sea.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Hopefully it is soon, hopefully it will be soon.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Ojalá sea pronto.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Ojalá sea pronto. Good. So ojalá you will hear and want to use very often, and also you use with this subjunctive tense. So like we said, you just want to listen out for when the mood tense is used, get interested in it, analyze why it's been used, think about why it's been used, think about how that fits in to the the image and the vision that you are getting of the mood tense and how and why it's used. It's something that you should enjoy and analyze, and the most interesting areas might be the optional uses, because with the optional uses of the mood tense, you can really give many different tones to what you're saying, whether it's humor, or sarcasm, or sincerity, irritation. There's a whole spectrum of feelings you can express with it, and these are best understood, explored in a live environment, practicing, listening to, and analyzing Spanish.
